💡 Key Takeaways
  • Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.
  • David Moyes credited Everton with giving him his first big break in management as he prepares to oversee a record-breaking 593rd match in charge of the club.
  • Moyes is set to surpass Harry Catterick's record of 592 games managed as Everton boss when his side make the trip to face Brentford in the Premier League.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Syndicated reporting provided by Stats Perform and reviewed by the SoccerNews editorial team.

David Moyes credited Everton with giving him his first big break in management as he prepares to oversee a record-breaking 593rd match in charge of the club.

Moyes is set to surpass Harry Catterick's record of 592 games managed as Everton boss when his side make the trip to face Brentford in the Premier League.

He first made the move to Merseyside in 2002 from Preston North End and remained in the Everton dugout for 11 years before replacing Alex Ferguson at Manchester United.

The 63-year-old went on to have spells at Real Sociedad, Sunderland and West Ham before returning to Everton in January 2025 to replace Sean Dyche.

During his two stints with the Toffees, Moyes has overseen 250 wins in all competitions (D155 L187), and his Everton side have started the 2026-27 campaign brightly.

Everton are seventh after signing off for the international break with a win over Coventry City, and Moyes wants that upward trajectory to continue in his milestone match.

"I'm really thrilled about it, but if I'm honest, it's not something I really think about," Moyes told reporters ahead of the trip to the Gtech Community Stadium.

"I've suddenly become the manager who has managed more Everton games than anyone before. That's a privilege and an honour to be put in that position.

"I have to thank the people who brought me to the club. When you take a chance on a young manager, you never know if it'll work, but they had faith and believed in me.

"I'm so thankful for the people around Everton because they've been so good for me.".

In a recent development, A presentation from Blues past and present. Leon Osman and James Tarkowski surprise David Moyes with a memento as he sets a newly introduced record for games managed for Everton Football Club (593). https://t.co/tzFuGeUhFW.

— Everton (@Everton) November 20, 2026.

Brentford boss Keith Andrews paid respect to the Scot.

According to recent reports, "I played against his Everton team. I've always had a lot of respect for him, even when I was a player," Andrews noted of the Everton boss.

"He's now an iconic manager of English football, with how long he's been involved and how successful he's been.".

Brentford know a win will see them leapfrog Everton in the Premier League, but they must do so without Igor Thiago, who was sent off against Brighton last time out.

Thiago was shown a red card for violent conduct in an incident with Chema Andres after a VAR review, with an appeal against the decision unanimously rejected.

Put to him that Callum Wilson could come in as a direct replacement in attack, Andrews added: "That would be your natural thinking.

According to recent reports, "We've got three players that have played that position and can play that position; wide players could become more central options. We have Fabio Carvalho coming back as well.

Sources indicate that "There are different ways that we can play, but Callum has obviously been champing at the bit. I do not doubt that he is going to get a decent number of minutes.".

With Thiago suspended, Andrews looks set to name Wilson as his starting striker against Everton, and it is not a bad replacement to have.

In a recent development, wilson has failed to score in the Premier League this season, but he does have a good record against Everton. Only against West Ham (12) has he scored more top-flight goals against than the Toffees (nine).

Barry's six goals are the most by a player in Everton's first 10 Premier League games of a season since Dominic Calvert-Lewin in 2020-21 (10), and the most by a non-English player for the club since Romelu Lukaku in 2016-17 (seven).

The Frenchman has scored (five) or assisted (one) six of the Toffees' last seven league goals, and you feel he will be key to his side's chances of victory here.

With 13 goal involvements from his first 13 matches of the 2026-27 season (10 goals, 3 assists), Thierno Barry looks like a man on a mission @jord_coll sat down exclusively with Everton striker to discuss his sensational start to the season, and how training with a former club legend has helped take him to new heights https://t.co/xZG7SZHbcO.

— Opta Analyst (@OptaAnalyst) November 20, 2026.

MATCH PREDICTION: BRENTFORD WIN.

Having won their first Premier League home game against Everton 1-0 in November 2021, Brentford are winless in their last four against them at the Gtech (D3 L1).

Andrews' side have, however, won four of their last seven Premier League games at the Gtech (D2 L1), and are looking for back-to-back home league wins for the first time in 2026, having last done so in November 2025 (three in a row).

But the Bees have won just one of their last 11 Premier League games that have come the matchday following an international break (D5 L5) – although that was the only such match they played on a Monday in this period, beating West Ham 2-0 in October 2025.

Everton, meanwhile, have lost just one of their last eight Premier League games against Brentford (W3 D4), though they are winless in their last four against them (D3 L1).

According to recent reports, this will be Everton's ninth top-flight game played on a Monday since the start of last season, three more than any other side in this time (Manchester United six). The Toffees have lost just one of their last seven on this day of the week (W2 D4), winning their last two away from home.

Moyes' men have won back-to-back Premier League games for the first time since between February and March, and are looking to win three in a row in the competition for the first time since May 2025.

#129470. Breaking: The curious case of Sebastien Pocognoli looks certain to have a grisly ending... the SFA have hired a dud

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)

Breaking: The curious case of Sebastien Pocognoli looks certain to have a grisly ending... the SFA have hired a dud

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.
  • Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.
  • Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.

Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.

In some of his other work written as he travelled across Europe, Fitzgerald also had a line about Switzerland, describing it as a ‘country where very few things begin, but many things end.’.

It is a curious quote and, like much of Fitzgerald’s work, is open to interpretation. As the man who also wrote The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, curiosity was a common theme.

As for the Curious Case of Sebastien Pocognoli, Switzerland may, indeed, be the country where everything came to an end.

What unfolded in St Gallen on Monday evening was a horror show. Scotland were battered 4-0 by Switzerland’s B team. There is no way to sugar-coat a result like that, no way to dress it up as anything other than an embarrassment. They played OK for half an hour and then fell apart.

Pocognoli claimed afterwards that there were positives to be taken and how some of Scotland’s football was the best they have produced across his six matches in charge.

Sebastien Pocognoli is facing serious questions after a miserable Nations League campaign.

It has been revealed that utter nonsense. That was a manager clutching at straws at the end of a Nations League campaign which has been an unmitigated disaster pretty much from start to finish.

Let’s go back to the very start here. After Steve Clarke had pushed the Scottish Football Association (SFA) into awarding him a new four-year contract, only to then walk away after the World Cup, it was a chance for a fresh start.

On the day when Pocognoli was unveiled as the new head coach in August, Ian Maxwell and Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief executive and chief football officer, were beaming with positivity.

They told us all how data and AI had been used in the recruitment process, and how several clubs across Europe had been chasing Pocognoli.

They clearly viewed it as a coup to have landed the 39-year-old Belgian, who had won a league title in his homeland with Union Saint-Gilloise before a short stint with Monaco.

Industry observers note that what would the data say now? Six games played, two wins, a draw and three defeats, five goals scored and ten conceded, seven points and a lousy third-placed finish in Group B1.

In a recent development, both of those wins came against a North Macedonian side who lost all six of their games. They were a pub team – and Scotland still struggled to beat them at Hampden last Friday night.

Pocognoli was unable to inspire any resistance as his side succumbed to defeat in St Gallen.

Scotland lost 7-0 on aggregate to Switzerland over the two games. Against Slovenia, a 0-0 draw on the opening day in Ljubljana was then followed with a woeful 2-1 defeat at Hampden.

According to recent reports, all of which begs a very simple question. Where, exactly, are the grounds for optimism here? How is this getting any better?

When Pocognoli arrived, he spoke about trying to change the style of play, get Scotland playing a more exciting brand of football, whilst bringing through a new generation of players.

It was not a rebuild. He inherited a group of players who were accustomed to success under Clarke and who qualified for three tournaments out of a possible four.

His remit was to help Scotland take the next step in major tournaments. With a more dynamic style of play, the job was to help the nation take the next step.

Industry observers note that there has been no revolution thus far. No evidence whatsoever that this coach is capable of delivering results nor a better style of play.

Sources indicate that there is no satisfaction to be taken in any of this. When Pocognoli was appointed, it was, in the eyes of this observer, an interesting and progressive move.

SFA chiefs Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell proudly unveil upcoming boss Pocognoli at Hampden.

Over the past 48 hours or so, there has been a lot of revisionism from some folk about Clarke. ‘Aye, the grass isn’t always greener...’.

That’s garbage. Clarke’s time was up with Scotland. He should never have been handed a new four-year deal in the first place. At least he did the right thing in resigning after the World Cup.

In a recent development, the whole thing was finished. The problem is that the SFA look like they have appointed a total dud as his successor. Both of those things can be true at the same time.

It is also worth remembering that the only reason we arrived at Pocognoli is because Clarke walked away. The SFA did not instigate any change.

The hiring of a new head coach was not a proactive change of direction, but a reactive move from an executive body who became accepting of Clarke’s limitations and allowed him to position them over a barrel.

Listen, there is nothing inherently wrong with using data and metrics in football. It’s the modern way. Using data to inform decisions and recruitment processes is smart business.

Industry observers note that but the data in itself is no guarantee of success. There are some intangibles in football, things which are harder to quantify. Like a manager who blindly sticks to a system which is patently ill-suited to the players at his disposal.

Things like leadership and communication skills. We can cut Pocognoli some slack in that English is not his first language. He comes across as a thoroughly decent and likeable chap. He’s doing his best. He wants to embrace the culture and makes an effort to sing the National Anthem.

Scotland's defeat arose from individual mistakes, a common theme during the Belgian's reign.

It has been revealed that all of that is undoubtedly to be welcomed. Good on him. But would anyone describe him as an inspirational figure?

When you listen to him speak, have you ever felt slightly confused in terms of the message he’s actually trying to get across?

Recent findings suggest that how must that sound in the dressing room? When Andy Robertson spoke post-match on Monday night, there was frustration in his voice.

According to recent reports, the captain insisted there is simply no time or patience with these things. Scotland need to deliver results now.

To be fair, there actually would be a degree of patience shown by the Tartan Army towards Pocognoli if there was something to actually believe in.

Recent findings suggest that there was a lot of goodwill towards him at the start. If there were signs across these last six games that he could deliver a more exciting team to watch, they would show patience.

Recent findings suggest that but on the basis of what we’ve seen so far, there’s been absolutely nothing to suggest he can move this team forward. Ask yourself a very simple question – do Scotland pass the eye test?

Are we seeing a team who are playing on the front foot and creating chances? The answer, obviously, is no.

Steve Clarke celebrates Scotland's win over Denmark a year ago... how fans miss such highs.

Many Scotland fans are now confronting the possibility that we might not even qualify for Euro 2028, a tournament which we are co-hosting.

By finishing third in the Nations League, we will now be in pot three for the Euro qualifiers and will face a more difficult group.

Beyond that, we would be relying on the back-door method of one of the best-placed home nations not to qualify directly.

Those Euro qualifiers will start in March of next year. Does Pocognoli even make it that far? Or should the SFA hold their hands up, admit they’ve made a mistake, and rectify it?

That feels unlikely. But on the basis of what we have seen over these first six games, it’s hard to see how this gets any better.

We are worse now than we were at the end under Clarke. Much, much worse. This is not teething problems. It’s a team who have regressed massively under a head coach who was supposed to move the whole thing forward.

On the eve of AC Milan’s game against Frosinone, Ruben Amorim spoke to the media at the usual pre-match press conference.

It has been revealed that the international break is officially over and Milan will be back in action tomorrow. After wins against Inter and Genoa, the goal is to make it three consecutive wins, although an in-form Frosinone side will be looking to make life difficult for them.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

In a recent development, amorim’s plan appears to be to field an attacking-minded starting eleven, picking up where he left off against Genoa. It’s certainly a bold plan as Frosinone will surely look to cause challenges on the counter, as also highlighted by Oliver in his prediction.

Speaking to the media at Milanello, Amorim shared his thoughts on the game, the status of the players after the international break, and the tactical solutions moving forward.

Sources indicate that “We as a club have a big responsibility. Fondazione Milan is really key because it reflects our values and helps the community. Our doors are always open for everyone. It’s also good for the players to see and live different realities.”.

On those involved in international duty….

“I think everyone is ready. Of course, we had to control the load during the week, because some of them travelled a lot. I’m really pleased with our players getting game time, because that’s the best way to maintain, so we are ready for the game.”.

On Pavlovic’s status and Frosinone’s style..

Recent findings suggest that “Starting with Pavlovic, he’s doing better. He will be in the squad. I don’t know if he will start or not, so I will see. He wants to play and I want him to play. We miss that fire that he has. Let’s see, but for sure he will be in the team.

Industry observers note that “Frosinone are fun to watch, they are the team that runs the most, and we are second so I think we can fight that. They are really good with 1v1s on the flanks. If you watch their games it’s hard to understand their movement. There is some logic in their chaos, but it’s hard to spot.

Sources indicate that “They play a different style, more direct, which allows them to have the ball more inside the box. So it’s going to be a really hard game. As I said against Venezia, there are some teams that we need to be really focused against because their styles can cause concerns.”.

Recent findings suggest that camarda is getting little game time, despite the Ramos struggles. Is a strong deputy striker missing?

In a recent development, “Two different questions. Of course we can say that one more option would be a good thing, but I think the struggles of Ramos are the struggles of the team. We are not reaching the final third, we are one of the worst teams in that sense. So we don’t have a lot of shots.

“I don’t want loads of shots outside the box, because it’s hard to score with those. We need to get into the box and we are not helping Ramos. What I saw against Genoa is that without Ramos, we wouldn’t have scored those goals. But again, we need to do better in the final third, my goal is to push the team forward. That’s my job.

Sources indicate that “It’s true that he’s working hard and doing a lot of good. I know that it’s not his sole job to press, we spent a lot of money on a player to score goals, but we are not doing enough to help him. We need to push the team forward.”.

Are you happy with the league standings so far? And against Genoa, you basically played with four attacking players. Can this be a solution for the future?

According to recent reports, “Starting with the last question, it depends on the opponents and the moment of the team. I don’t believe that playing with more attackers means you will reach the final third more. Sometimes you get that effect from having more midfielders, for example. We are always going to change in some matches depending on the opponent.

It has been revealed that “On the first question, it’s difficult to say. I think that we have grown as a team quite fast, but I’m not pleased with the overall situation. We need to be so much better and as such, I’m not pleased with where we are in the standings. But of course, I need to say that I’m happy with how the players have worked.”.

Sources indicate that during the break, we saw Camarda scoring for the U21s. Could a loan be the right solution?

“I was a young player myself once too. A young player wants everything really badly, which is a good thing. That noted, he needs time to adapt, it’s really hard to play for a club like Milan. You just said there is pressure on Ramos, imagine what it’s like for Camarda.

Sources indicate that “I don’t know what will happen in January, but he needs to be focused on these games. Everything can change in just a few weeks.

“I’m really happy with how he has been since he returned from international duty, I heard that Baldini spoke with him at length (as Baldini stated himself), and he returned in a happier mood. I understand the question about January, but January is so far away right now.”.

The feeling is that the team is struggling to keep control at the end of the games….

“Sometimes even when we are winning, we have dropped the levels in every action of the game. I think we are controlling everything better, you saw it in the second half against Genoa without spending a lot of energy, but I think it’s all connected to the attack.

“If we don’t create danger when we are leading, we will struggle a bit to kill the games. Of course, we need to address that and we are working on it.”.

On Musah as a left-back and if more versatile players will be signed….

“That was a specific situation. I don’t know and I’m not going to tell you guys what we are thinking about January. I wanted a right-footed player against Genoa. You saw the runs of Rabiot, so I wanted someone right-footed to pass the ball on immediately.

It has been revealed that “Musah is not going to play as a left-back tomorrow, I can tell you that, but it’s an option. I like to have players who can play in several positions.”.

“I think it helps any player to feel the confidence from the club. I think it’s clear that was done with the fresh contract. Then I also told you when he wasn’t playing that he’s really important for us. I can tell you today that Pulisic perhaps is the one player we cannot replace.

“The movement in between the lines he brings, we simply don’t have another Pulisic. His absence is always felt a lot, so from that you can understand how crucial he is for us. He doesn’t talk a lot, but he lets the pitch do the talking.

“I would put him in the same category as Rabiot. Players who are on another level. I don’t like speaking about individuals, but I think everyone can see this.”.

Can the January transfer window serve to raise the team’s ambition?

“That is the biggest mistake of the big clubs. Looking at the table and deciding whether to invest or not. I think the key is to have a long-term plan. Stick with your plan. We have one and everything is very clear.

In a recent development, “Trying to become a champion by spending money is the biggest mistake. The key is following your strategy. I look at the table to evaluate the process as a whole, not to decide whether to spend a lot on signings.”.

Are you keeping track of your players so they don’t stay up late at night playing GTA?

“I will let my friend Gennaro Gattuso respond. Jokes aside, I don’t care.”.

Industry observers note that is a winner a dreamer who never gives up? Are you a dreamer?

Sources indicate that “I wouldn’t call it a dream but the goal is to win every game. If you look at my journey, every club I chose, I clearly am a dreamer [laughs]. I really want to be part of this club for the rest of my career, but I also know that I need to prove myself.

“I’m a dreamer, yes, but also very focused on the goal.”.

Tech Report: Rainforest adaptation in late Homo erectus from southern China

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 56 min read (11149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~56 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2.
  • Sources indicate that early and late H.
  • Establishing the environmental context of H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that homo erectus represents one of the longest-persisting hominin species, with a geographic range from Africa to eastern Eurasia from approximately 1.9 million years ago1 to 108 thousand years ago (ka)2. Despite this, there are still large gaps in our understanding of the adaptation capabilities of this species and the extent of its persistence in China. Assumptions over ecological preferences based on the Trinil3, Sangiran4 and Ngandong2 (in Java) open woodland–grassland mosaics have persisted, combined with limited direct stable carbon isotope measurements in Asia. Here we present a rich temporal and environmental context for nine hominin teeth, eight of which were morphologically and genetically identified as H. erectus5, found in two sister caves in Guangxi province, southern China. We modelled 43 radiometric ages from five dating techniques to establish a timeline for H. erectus presence in this region. Stable and clumped isotopes and trace elements from teeth were used to establish the dominant environments and their behavioural responses. We show that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, which is substantially more recent than previously established in this region for unequivocally H. erectus fossils at approximately 400 ka. The evidence suggests that they were persisting in closed rainforest ecosystems, thought to be the domain of only Homo sapiens, and were demonstrating long-term mobility and ecological flexibility. This evidence challenges the assumptions over the ecological preferences and behavioural limitations of H. erectus.

Sources indicate that early and late H. erectus finds in East and Southeast Asia represent a key part of the hominin evolutionary history of the Asian region, with China sitting in an important location to understand the dispersal, interactions and adaptations of this species6,7,8. There is a rich fossil record for H. erectus in China in Yuanmou (1.7 million years ago)9,10,11, Gongwangling (1.6 million years ago)12, Zhoukoudian (780–400 ka)13, Nanjing (approximately 650 ka)14 and Hexian (410 ka)15 (Supplementary Information 1). However, most of these sites are located in north and central China, with reliably identified and dated H. erectus fossils being conspicuously rare in southern China, especially during the Middle Pleistocene. This makes it particularly challenging to establish their ecological preferences. Furthermore, evidence of younger H. erectus (less than 400 ka) is almost entirely absent from China. This temporal gap is particularly striking given that H. erectus persisted in Java until 117–108 ka at Ngandong2, raising fundamental questions about the species’ distribution, ecological adaptations and ultimate fate in mainland China.

Establishing the environmental context of H. erectus is essential for understanding the species’ ecological flexibility and adaptive capabilities. The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in woodland refugia as rainforests expanded across the region, raising questions about whether encroaching closed-canopy forests contributed to the species’ eventual extinction2,16. Yet, there have been very few stable isotope studies on H. erectus evidence, as the material is often limited by diagenetic alteration3. Recent work has debated whether non-H. sapiens Middle Pleistocene hominins possessed the adaptive capabilities to exploit tropical rainforest environments17,18. Studying the forested landscapes of tropical southern China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene19 thus provides a crucial test case for assessing H. erectus ecological adaptations. Furthermore, understanding mobility patterns through techniques such as strontium isotope analysis can reveal how these populations used their landscapes and how they connected with contemporaneous populations across broader regional scales20,21.

Industry observers note that since the Pleistocene, tropical forest and grassland environments in southern China have provided a critical biogeographical corridor for faunal dispersals between northern latitudes and insular Southeast Asia22,23,24. The karst landscapes and cave systems of the region have yielded abundant Pleistocene faunal assemblages, yet there is at the moment no clear evidence that H. erectus was part of the Stegodon–Ailuropoda fauna in this region6. This raises questions as to whether the absence of H. erectus in southern China, particularly during the late Middle Pleistocene, is a consequence of ecological constraints preventing H. erectus from exploiting southern China’s tropical forest environments18, representing an effective biogeographic barrier25, or results from other factors such as an imbalance in research intensity7, a reflection of real absence of the species in the region due to alternative dispersal routes through the Tibetan corridor6, the absence of secure dating data on many out-of-context teeth, the misidentification of fragmentary remains (particularly with morphologically similar Pongo teeth26), taphonomic and preservation biases in tropical environments18, lower population densities leading to reduced fossil representation27 or the occupation of an ecological niche that is not readily preserved in cave deposits18. Distinguishing between these scenarios requires well-dated, robustly identified hominin fossils with detailed environmental context—evidence that has been lacking.

To provide a temporal and environmental context for the eight H. erectus teeth6 from Baxian and Naxian caves in southern China (Fig. 1, Supplementary Information 2 and 3 and Extended Data Figs. 1–3), we used five independent dating techniques to constrain the sediments: post-infrared infrared-stimulated luminescence (pIR-IRSL) dating of feldspars, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating of quartz (Supplementary Information 4), uranium-series (U-series) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 5), coupled U-series–electron spin resonance (US-ESR) dating of fossil teeth (Supplementary Information 6) and U-series dating of carbonate capping flowstones (Supplementary Information 7), all integrated through the use of two Bayesian age models—ChronoModel and OxCal (Supplementary Information 8). Environmental reconstruction was achieved through faunal analysis (Supplementary Information 3), bulk and sequential stable isotope analysis of faunal and H. erectus tooth enamel (Supplementary Information 9) and clumped isotope thermometry of cave sediments (Supplementary Information 10). Finally, we assessed individual mobility patterns through laser-ablation trace element mapping and strontium isotope analysis of hominin tooth enamel, integrated with a regional strontium isoscape constructed using random forest machine learning to identify potential source regions (Supplementary Information 11). These multiple lines of evidence, replicated across laboratories in China and Australia, provide, to our knowledge, the first comprehensive temporal, environmental and behavioural context for late H. erectus in southern China.

The Naxian and Baxian caves, located 15 km apart and situated 13 km to the northwest and 20 km to the north of Chongzuo City, respectively, are connected by a straight karst valley corridor (Fig. 1, Extended Data Fig. 1a,b,e,f and Supplementary Information 2). They are both horizontal caves at 226 and 218 m above sea level, positioned 5–7 m above the valley floor (Extended Data Fig. 2), with small fossil chambers at the rear of each cave (Fig. 2). The chambers contain remarkably similar dense, cemented, cataclastic breccias that have yielded a combined total of over 18,000 mammalian fossils, which were initially accumulated by porcupines28, including hominin remains (Supplementary Information 2). The fossil-bearing breccias (Extended Data Fig. 3) were capped by thick flowstone and underlain by younger mixed sediments (Extended Data Fig. 1d,h). This similarity suggests deposition under comparable environmental conditions.

Of the resulting 45 radiometric ages from both caves (Extended Data Figs. 4–7), 43 were modelled and given similar modelled age estimates (OxCal: 312–161 ka; ChronoModel: 324–184 ka at 2σ uncertainties; Extended Data Fig. 8), but the ChronoModel results were used owing to their greater outlier robustness and more reliable lower age limit. These results indicate that the age of H. erectus fossil evidence lies between 324 and 184 ka for the Baxian caves, and between 319 and 241 ka for the Naxian caves. These error limits are overlapping and broadly contemporaneous, and indicate a 95% probability that H. erectus was in this area sometime between 324 and 184 ka (see Supplementary Information 4–8 for all dating tables, data and discussion of limitations, uncertainties and choice of model; Fig. 3). The overlapping age uncertainties for the caves of approximately 78,000 years suggest a contemporaneous or near-contemporaneous presence on this landscape. The modelled ages are consistent across all five dating techniques within their respective uncertainties, providing robust constraints on the timing of H. erectus presence in this region.

Sources indicate that the faunal assemblages from the Baxian and Naxian caves are taxonomically diverse and remarkably similar in composition (Supplementary Information 3 and Extended Data Fig. 3). Both assemblages include numerous taxa that have since become locally extinct, including Pongo, Elephas and rhinoceros Dicerorhinus, though most remain extant elsewhere in Asia. Notably, H. erectus, Stegodon and ‘Megalovis’ are globally extinct. Habitat preference analysis indicates that both assemblages are strongly dominated by forest-dwelling taxa (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with predominantly forested landscapes during the time of deposition.

It has been revealed that the plant-equivalent stable carbon isotope values for the Baxian faunal teeth, after correction for species-specific diet-to-enamel enrichment factors based on body mass29 (Supplementary Information 9), range from −31.5 to −23.0‰ (average = −27.6 ± 1.87‰ (1σ)), while lower values observed at the Naxian cave range from −34.0 to −25.1‰ (average = −29.4 ± 2.45‰ (1σ)). Both assemblages yield values well below the dense-canopy forest threshold of −27.5‰ (ref. 28), with no evidence of C4 plant consumption or even C3–C4 intermediate signatures (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 9). These data indicate that the fauna at both sites derived their dietary carbon exclusively from C3 vegetation, with the frequency of canopy-related values exceeding those reported for equatorial African rainforest systems29 and being comparable to that documented for western Amazonian forests30,31,32. This pattern is particularly notable given that several of the taxa represented in the assemblages are known elsewhere to exploit mixed C3–C4 resources or to incorporate substantial C4-derived inputs into their diets in more open environments16.

Independent oxygen isotope (δ18O) and clumped isotope (Δ47) analyses further support these environmental reconstructions, indicating humid tropical conditions with higher precipitation and cooler temperatures than modern values in this region (Extended Data Fig. 9 and Supplementary Information 9 and 10).

In a recent development, three H. erectus teeth from the Naxian cave (NX-B1, NX-B2 and NX-A1) show similarly low isotopic values, with carbon values ranging from −15.0 to −14.0‰, which fall at the boundary between dense-canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. Although the dataset is limited (n = 3) and currently restricted to the Naxian locality, these values are fully consistent with those observed across the much larger faunal assemblage and fall within the range expected for consumers deriving their dietary carbon from closed-canopy C3 vegetation, demonstrating that these late H. erectus populations exploited tropical rainforest resources.

Industry observers note that high-resolution trace element mapping on one H. erectus individual from the Baxian cave (PA1799) yielded 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220 (Supplementary Information 11 and Extended Data Fig. 10), while three H. erectus teeth sampled from the Naxian cave highlighted overlapping but distinct ranges. All four individuals indicate either movement between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood (2–6 years), corresponding to the period of tooth formation.

A regional strontium isoscape for southern China and northern Southeast Asia33 (Supplementary Information 11) reveals substantial spatial heterogeneity in predicted 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with the local Baxian–Naxian region characterized by relatively homogeneous values (0.710–0.715), reflecting the dominant Carboniferous–Permian limestone karst geology (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10). More radiogenic signatures (0.717–0.723) occur to the west and northwest in mountainous areas underlain by Precambrian and Palaeozoic metamorphic rocks, while intermediate to more radiogenic values (0.715–0.720) characterize regions to the south, including the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

Geographic assignment probability maps generated for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in the human tooth profiles indicate that these H. erectus individuals may have moved between the local limestone karst regions and more distant areas during childhood, with the most radiogenic signatures potentially pointing towards areas as far afield as northern Vietnam, which connect southern China with mainland Southeast Asia (Figs. 1 and 3 and Extended Data Fig. 10).

Recent findings suggest that our results demonstrate that H. erectus was present in southern China between 324 and 184 ka (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 8), representing, to our knowledge, the youngest reliably dated occurrence of this species in China and the first with robust chronological constraints from southern China. The integration of multiple independent dating techniques combined with Bayesian age modelling provides unprecedented temporal resolution for late H. erectus in mainland Asia. These findings fundamentally alter our understanding of the species’ persistence and distribution in China, extending the documented record by more than 200,000 years beyond the previous youngest occurrences in Hexian and Nanjing14,15, and establishing southern China as a key region for late-surviving populations during the late Middle Pleistocene (for example, ref. 19).

According to recent reports, the temporal importance of this discovery extends beyond simply filling a chronological gap. The age uncertainty range of 324–184 ka places these H. erectus populations at some point within marine isotope stages 9 through 6, raising intriguing questions about potential contemporaneity or overlap with Homo longi (Denisovans) identified in Cobra cave (Laos)34, Baishiya cave (Tibetan Plateau)35, Harbin (northeast China)36,37,38 and the Penghu Channel off the western shore of Taiwan39. The temporal proximity of these various hominin populations across China during the late Middle Pleistocene suggests a more complex biogeographical landscape than previously recognized, with multiple hominin lineages potentially coexisting across different ecological zones and elevational gradients.

It has been revealed that moreover, the environmental context revealed by our multi-proxy analyses challenges prevailing assumptions about late H. erectus ecological constraints and mobility patterns. The combined evidence demonstrates unequivocally that these late H. erectus populations exploited closed-canopy tropical rainforest environments and may have conducted long-distance movement beyond the local karst terrain during childhood. The ecological implications of this rainforest use and mobility are profound. Archaeological evidence has so far suggested that H. sapiens was the only member of our genus to specialize in the regular exploitation of these environments18, as early as 150 ka in western Africa40,41. In Southeast Asia, recent isotopic observations of declines in C4 environments and expansion of rainforest in the Middle to early Late Pleistocene have been associated with the disappearance of non-H. sapiens hominin taxa42,43, seemingly unable to shift from mixed savannah–woodland habitats to these increasingly closed forests16,44. However, our data directly challenge this view by demonstrating that H. erectus was not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments (Fig. 3) and that long-distance mobility into these environments may have been a common behavioural pattern rather than exceptional behaviour by isolated individuals.

These findings contrast markedly with Early and Middle Pleistocene H. erectus occupations at Trinil3 and Sangiran in Java4 (Extended Data Fig. 9b). The youngest Javanese H. erectus at Ngandong2 persisted in relatively open woodland refugia2, leading to suggestions that expanding rainforests may have contributed to the species’ eventual extinction in Java2,16. Among early hominin-bearing sites in East and Southeast Asia (Extended Data Fig. 9b), the Naxian and Baxian cave results most closely resemble those from Lida Ajer, Sumatra (73–63 ka), an early H. sapiens site also characterized by closed-canopy rainforest45. This demonstrates that H. erectus was, at minimum, capable of persisting among rainforest fauna, even if such habitats did not represent its optimal ecological niche.

Areas in northern Vietnam, such as the Red River valley (Figs. 1 and 3), have long been recognized as a critical biogeographical corridor connecting the karst uplands of southern China with the lowlands of mainland Southeast Asia24. The limited strontium isotope evidence tentatively suggests that late H. erectus populations may have been utilizing similar corridors for seasonal movements, long-distance migrations or resource procurement. This large range (potentially around 250 km) through mostly enclosed environments challenges assumptions about the limited ranging behaviour of H. erectus and suggests behavioural sophistication in landscape use.

Our findings collectively demonstrate that late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus was present in southern China, surviving contemporaneously with H. longi and exhibiting considerable ecological and behavioural flexibility. Rather than being restricted to open savanna or woodland habitats, as traditionally assumed, these populations persisted in closed-canopy tropical rainforests while simultaneously engaging in potential long-distance mobility across diverse ecological and geological landscapes. This evidence challenges the characterization of H. erectus as a species unable to exploit complex tropical forest environments. Whether these adaptations were specific to the late-surviving populations in southern China alone remains to be seen, but further stable isotope work on other Middle Pleistocene sites is vital to address this question. However, the presence of morphologically and genetically confirmed H. erectus in southern China between 324 and 184 ka, combined with the environmental and suggested mobility evidence, is sufficient to necessitate a re-evaluation of the species’ adaptive capabilities, biogeographical range and ultimate fate in mainland Asia.

Recent findings suggest that the caves were discovered using local knowledge and targeted reconnaissance hunting for breccia in the rear chambers. The locations of test pits within the caves were selected on the basis of these reconnaissance surveys. Excavation grids were based on the shape of cave passages and distribution of fossil-rich deposits. Jackhammers were used to break blocks of fossil breccia, and the fossils were extracted using geological hammers. Fine cleaning, identification and cataloguing were conducted in the laboratories at Shandong University and the Institute of Vertebrate Palaeontology and Palaeoanthropology (IVPP).

The fossil-bearing breccia and associated sediments from the fossil chambers of both caves were sampled in situ under subdued red-light conditions (Fig. 2a,d) and were processed using standard sample purification procedures for quartz and feldspar separation including a 40% and 10% wash in hydrofluoric acid for 45 and 10 mins, respectively46. Single aliquots of 90–125 µm feldspar and 180–212 µm quartz or feldspar grains were processed in a Riso TL-DA-20 equipped with an automated DASH set-up, a dual-laser single-grain attachment47 and a blue- and ultraviolet-sensitive Electron Tube photo-multiplier tube (PDM9107Q-AP-TTL-03), using either a blue filter pack (Schott BG-39, 2 mm, and Corning 7-59, 4 mm) for feldspars or U340 filters (2 × Hoya U340, 3.5 mm) for quartz. Data were collected using Sequence Pro v.4.65 and analysed in Analyst v.4.57, DRAC v.1.3 and on spreadsheets designed in Microsoft Excel 365 v.2607. Feldspar equivalent doses were corrected according to the results of the anomalous fading tests (using a weighted mean fading rate of 2.0 ± 0.2% per decade)48, but no residual corrections were undertaken, and the equivalent doses for both feldspar and quartz were then run through either a central age model for the single-aliquot results or a minimum age model49 to identify the single-grain population that experienced the most bleaching before burial. All luminescence analysis was conducted at the ‘Traps’ luminescence dating facility at Macquarie University in Sydney, Australia.

Measurements of 238U, 235U, 232Th and 40K were estimated using Geiger–Muller multi-counter beta counting and thick-source alpha counting of dried and powdered sediment samples in the laboratory, combined with in situ gamma spectrometry in the field. The corresponding (dry) beta and gamma dose rates were obtained using the conversion factors in ref. 50 and the beta-dose attenuation factors in ref. 51. Cosmic-ray dose rates were estimated from previously published relationships52, making allowance for the sediment overburden at the sample locality (ranging from 3.99 to 0.20 m), the altitude (ranging from 2,000 to 176 m above sea level) and geomagnetic latitude and longitude of the sampling sites.

Recent findings suggest that seven H. erectus teeth from the Naxian (n = 6) and Baxian (n = 1) caves were analysed for U-series dating across two laboratories in China and Australia. U-series measurements were undertaken using a laser-ablation multi-collector inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometer (MC-ICP-MS) at the Geoarchaeology and Archaeometry Research Group (GARG), Southern Cross University, according to protocols in ref. 53 and in a Neptune MC-ICP-MS at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University according to refs. 54,55. Laser ablation (at Southern Cross University) was performed with a Latest Wave Research 213 nm laser, and thorium (230Th, 232Th) and uranium (234U, 235U, 238U) isotopes were measured on a Thermo Neptune XT MC-ICP-MS. Teeth were ablated using rasters of 5 min each and were measured with standards before and after. Uranium and thorium were separated using conventional anion-exchange chromatography at Nanjing, and the U–Th solution was then introduced into the MC-ICP-MS via a DSN-100 desolvation nebulizer system. Isotopic ratios were measured using a detector configuration that allows for the simultaneous measurement of U and Th isotopes56,57.

In a recent development, one H. erectus tooth and one Pongo tooth from the Baxian cave (n = 2) were selected for coupled ESR and U-series dating at GARG, Southern Cross University. Enamel fragments from each tooth were separated using a hand-held diamond saw following the protocol developed in ref. 58. Fragments were then measured at room temperature on a Freiberg MS5000 ESR X-band spectrometer at a modulation amplitude of 0.1 mT, 10 scans, 2 mW power, 100 G sweep and 100 kHz modulation frequency. Each fragment was irradiated, following exponentially increasing irradiation times. Sediment elemental concentrations, external beta and gamma dose rate contributions, and water content were obtained from in situ measurements. The external beta-dose rates have been extrapolated from the U, Th and K contents measured on a portion of sediment sub-sample (approximately 8 g). The external gamma dose rates were determined in situ using a portable gamma spectrometer at each site. The equivalent doses were estimated using Matlab-based MCdose software v.2.0.

Separate sub-samples were hand-drilled from the fresh cross-section of the in situ capping flowstones from Naxian and Baxian caves and processed at the Radiogenic Isotope Facility, University of Queensland (n = 6), and six soda straws and one sample of secondary calcite cement were processed at the School of Geography Science, Nanjing Normal University (n = 7). The powdered sub-samples were subjected to chemical treatment and isotopic measurements by mass spectrometry56. U-series dating of the speleothem samples were conducted at the University of Queensland using a Nu Plasma MC-ICP-MS, and analytical procedures followed previous publications for MC-ICP-MS57,58,59. The 230Th/234U ages were calculated using Isoplot EX 3.75 (ref. 60) and half-lives of 75,690 years for 230Th and 245,250 years for 234U (ref. 61). U-series dating of the speleothem samples was carried out at Nanjing Normal University using a Neptune MC-ICP-MS. U-series ages were calculated using the half-lives of 75,584 years for 230Th and 245,620 years for 234U (ref. 62). Non-radiogenic 230Th was corrected using an assumed bulk-Earth atomic 230Th/232Th ratio of (4.4 ± 2.2) × 10−6 (refs. 54,55).

Two Bayesian modelling programs were used to analyse selected independent age estimates (n = 43) (Supplementary Information 8) and to evaluate the uncertainties associated with the combined dating techniques applied to both sites (Supplementary Tables 7–15): OxCal (v.4.4.4, available at https://c14.arch.ox.ac.uk/oxcal.html)63 and ChronoModel (v.3.2.7, https://chronomodel.com/)64. The analyses incorporated the probability distributions of individual ages, constraints imposed by stratigraphic relationships and the reported minimum or maximum nature of some of the individual age estimates. Each individual age was included as a Gaussian distribution (with mean and s.d. defined by the age estimate and their associated uncertainties), and the resulting age ranges for each phase of deposition were presented at 2σ. OxCal allows the identification of boundary ages between each layer to constrain the fossil layer and ChronoModel was applied to assess the extent to which identical or similar data could be obtained. Both modelling results have been presented for transparency.

Three H. erectus specimens from the Naxian cave, as well as 47 faunal teeth from the Baxian cave and 38 from the Naxian cave (n = 41 in total), were taxonomically identified and prepared for stable isotope analysis, following established preparation methods65 (but see refs. 66,67). The resulting δ13C and δ18O values were measured using a ThermoFisher MAT253+ in six separate measurement blocks per sample at the Earth and Environmental Sciences’ Stable Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory at the University of Queensland. The evolved CO2 gases from the Naxian teeth were analysed for carbon and oxygen isotope compositions using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer housed at the Key Laboratory of Archaeological Sciences and Technology, Shandong University. Stable isotope measurements on the three H. erectus teeth were carried out at the Service de spectrométrie de masse isotopique du Muséum national d’Histoire naturelle, Paris, and analysed using a Thermo Delta V Advantage isotope ratio mass spectrometer. To assess isotopic differences among sites, we applied non-parametric and multivariate tests. For univariate comparisons, Kruskal–Wallis tests revealed highly significant differences in both δ13Ccarbon source (χ² = 181.5, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) and δ18O (χ² = 114.4, d.f. = 6, P < 0.001) among sites. All statistical analyses were conducted using the open-source program R software (v.4.5.1)68.

According to recent reports, three in situ samples were collected in bulk (CBAX2, CBAX3, CBAX4) from the breccia at Baxian and the clumped isotope analysis was undertaken in the Macquarie GeoAnalytical Stable Isotope Facility using a ThermoFisher dual-inlet MAT253+ mass spectrometer. The results were processed using the Easotope software package69. The final Δ47 value for each sample was then averaged and reported with 95% confidence intervals, before temperatures were calculated using the calibration in ref. 70 for 90 °C reactions. Using these temperatures, the oxygen isotopic composition of the precipitating fluid (δ18Ofluid) was calculated using the equation in ref. 71.

One H. erectus tooth from Baxian was sectioned with a high-precision diamond saw and polished to a smoothness of greater than 5 μm. Laser ablation combined with ICP-MS was used for trace elemental mapping analyses using an ESI NWR193 coupled to an Agilent 7900 ICP-MS at GARG, Southern Cross University, according to the procedures in refs. 19,72. A laser spot size of 40 μm, a scan speed of 80 μm s−¹, a laser intensity of 60% (approximately 1 J mm−2) and a total integration time of 0.50 s were used to produce data points that corresponded to a pixel size of approximately 40 × 40 μm. NIST610 and NIST612 (certified standard reference materials) were used to assess signal drift. Strontium isotope analysis (87Sr/86Sr) was conducted on four H. erectus teeth: one from Baxian cave and three from Naxian cave, also using laser-ablation MC-ICP-MS at the GARG facility. Enamel fragments were carefully extracted from regions showing low uranium concentrations and distinct elemental signatures from the surrounding dentine according to the mapping results. To contextualize the 87Sr/86Sr values obtained and assess potential mobility patterns, a regional strontium isoscape was constructed for southern China and northern Southeast Asia. The isoscape modelling was based on random forest ensemble machine learning analyses adapted from the original script developed in ref. 33 and followed the method fully described in ref. 21.

All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning were based on the global bioavailable strontium database in ref. 33 and all R scripts necessary for generating isoscapes are available at Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21131183)74.

K.E.W., Y.Z., R.J.-B., W.L., W.W., C.J., Y.W., W.Y., Y.P. and L.Y. explored and excavated the sites and collected faunal and dating samples, K.E.W. conducted the luminescence dating, R.J.-B., W.Y. and Q.S. conducted the U-series and coupled U-series–ESR dating of the teeth, and J.-x.Z. and Q.S. conducted the U-series measurements on the speleothem. R.J.-B. conducted the trace element analysis and V.B. conducted the isoscape work. M.Q., S.M., L.H. and A.-M.B. conducted stable isotope analysis on the fossil teeth, and N.B. and P.R. conducted isotope data analysis. M.Q. and S.M. conducted the clumped isotope analysis of the breccia, Y.Z., Y.P. and A.-M.B. analysed the fauna and K.E.W. designed the dating approach and conducted the Bayesian modelling. R.K., C.Z., W.L., R.D.Á., F.W., Z.W. and Q.F. worked on the hominin teeth. Finally, K.E.W., R.J.-B., W.L. and Y.Z. wrote the paper, with contributions from all co-authors.

In a recent development, a-d Naxian cave, a and b the cave – location marked with a red star - is situated on the outer cone of a karst inselberg located close to a highway. c a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology of the cave with the small entrance and flowstone step that leads into the stalagmite chamber dense with speleothem, a larger chamber with narrow and high ceilings and terminating with a small fossil chamber with breccia, d the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain by a younger underlying mixed material below. e-h Baxian Cave e and f the cave is also situated on the outer edge of a karst cone with the limestone corridor than connects both caves, cave location is marked with a red star, g a montage of images to demonstrate the speleology and sedimentology of the cave from the wide and high entrance to the narrower and smaller passage that lead to the confined fossil chamber, h the fossil bearing breccia at the highest point of the cave capped with flowstone and underlain with the younger underlying mixed material. There is a remarkable similarity between the stratigraphy and sedimentology of these deposits and associated fossils (d, h).

According to recent reports, a Naxian profile, b Baxian profile illustrating the changing speleology and cave deposits from the upper fossil chambers down to the entrances. Baxian is longer than Naxian but slopes at a lesser angle than the steeper Naxian. Images illustrate the main features found in both caves including a wider chamber and smaller fossil chambers. The images of the fossil chambers are taken from a 3D models of the caves (Supplementary Information 2 for links).

The horizontal grey banded region denotes a range within 2 sigma of the central point determined using a central age model (CAM). The blue banded region denotes a range within 2 sigma of the minimum age as determined using the minimum age model (MAM). The equivalent dose (De) can be obtained by defining a line that starts on the zero point on the x-axis and projects to the curved axis on the right hand side of the plot, while the uncertainty and precession are read vertically projected onto the y axis.

The red dashed box indicates the sampling location, c sampled section of flowstone from Naxian (CNAX-F1B) before processing, the knife tip indicates the calcite layer to be sampled, d sampled section of flowstone from Baxian (CBAXC-F2a) before processing, e sampled section of flowstone from Naxian (CNAX-F1) before processing, the knife indicates the calcite layer to be sampled, f soda straws sampled from the breccia in Naxian before processing, see the associated scale bar for sizes g secondary calcite cement sampled from Naxian breccia see the associated scale bar for size.

a: Combined p-value (physical uranium uptake parameter) trajectories for enamel and dentine illustrating the relative goodness-of-fit of uranium-uptake histories over the modelled time interval. The enamel curve indicates a broader temporal sensitivity, while dentine exhibits steeper p-value responses reflecting higher susceptibility to uranium migration. b: Normalised uranium-uptake curves for enamel (red) and dentine (green) showing contrasting U-uptake kinetics, with enamel characterised by delayed uptake and dentine by more rapid early incorporation. c: Frequency distribution of modelled ages generated under the US-ESR age model, illustrating the central tendency and dispersion of the Monte-Carlo age simulations used to derive the final age estimate, d H. erectus tooth from Baxian that was dated using US-ESR techniques (Supplementary Information 6).

It has been revealed that a and b are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr for the five dating techniques modelled according to Oxcal and applied to the sediments and fossils of Naxian (a) and Baxian (b) caves. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The techniques are colour coded according to the legend and organised into the unit in which they were sampled from – the flowstone, breccia or underlying clay. Some of the techniques represent minimum ages (such as the US ages on teeth) and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the right, while other represent maximum ages such as the pIR-IRSL single aliquot dating of feldspars and contain a colour coded arrow pointing the left. The thick black horizontal boxes with dashed lines represent the boundary ages (and errors) estimated by the modelling. The boundary ages quoted represent the upper and lower age ranges for the breccia units in both caves. c and d are the dating results (n = 43) as separate age estimates in kyr modelling according to Chronomodel for the same five dating techniques. Data are presented as mean values +/− SD. The individual sample events have been organised into three phases; breccia deposition (including fossil and sediment ages), overlying flowstone precipitation and underlying clay deposition with each phase represented by a different plot. The timescale goes from more recent on the right (50 ka written as -50000) to oldest on the left (400 ka written as -400000). For Baxian (c) we have used the age uncertainty at 2 σ (95%) of the fossil teeth dated using US-ESR (H. erectus and Pongo), resulting in an age of 324-184 ka. For Naxian (d), the fossils are all dated using US only so represent minimum ages, so instead we have used the period between the overlying flowstone (as the minimum age) and the youngest soda straw in the breccia (as the maximum age) both at 2 σ (95%) uncertainty to constrain the age of breccia deposition at 319-241 ka. The use of Chronomodel compared to Oxcal has accentuated similar events and reduced the younger age uncertainty by around 20 kyr. The overlapping uncertainty between the two caves has been used to represent a Homo erectus presence at some point between 324-184 ka.

Recent findings suggest that a Taxon-specific δ13Ccarbon source values in relation to vegetation type. δ13Ccarbon source (plant-equivalent values; ‰ VPDB at Baxian (324-184) and Naxian (319-241 ka). Shaded background areas indicate ecological zones: dense canopy forest (dark green), C3 vegetation (light green), and C4 grassland (yellow). The unshaded interval between C3 and C4 represents the C3–C4 intermediate zone. This framework allows direct comparison of faunal isotopic signatures against expected vegetation regimes. A large proportion of taxa from both sites fall within the dense canopy forest zone, supporting the interpretation of closed-canopy rainforest environments. The H. erectus values (red stars) fall within the C3 forest domain and plot at the boundary between dense canopy forest and more open C3 vegetation. b Vegetation zone proportions at hominin-bearing sites in Southeast Asia and South China. Proportional distribution of faunal δ13Ccarbon source values assigned to vegetation zones (dense canopy C3, open C3, C3–C4 intermediate, and C4). Bars show the relative contributions of each zone across six hominin-bearing sites: Trinil4, Sangiran5, Cobra Cave34,73, Duoi U’Oi74, Lida Ajer45,75, Baxian and Naxian. Baxian and Naxian are dominated by C3 signals, with substantial contributions from dense canopy vegetation, while Trinil and Sangiran show higher proportions of intermediate and C4 values, reflecting more open habitats. Lida Ajer is strongly weighted toward dense canopy values, consistent with closed rainforest settings. Together, these results illustrate marked ecological contrasts between late H. erectus contexts in China and Javanese sites, as well as affinities between Naxian and the rainforest environment of early H. sapiens at Lida Ajer75,76,77.

a Trace element distribution maps of the Baxian H. erectus tooth. LA-ICP-MS elemental maps showing the distribution of (i) 7Li/43Ca, (ii) 88Sr/43Ca, (iii) 138Ba/43Ca, and (iv) 238U/43Ca ratios normalised to calcium across a longitudinal section of the tooth. All maps show both enamel (upper/left portion, blue-green colours) and dentine (lower/right portion, predominantly dark red). The colour scales are optimised to visualise variation within the enamel tissue. Dark red areas in the dentine for Sr, Ba, and U maps indicate significantly elevated concentrations due to post-depositional diagenetic uptake from the burial environment, rendering these tissues unsuitable for life history reconstruction. In contrast, the enamel tissue displays lower concentrations and visible banding patterns, particularly Ba/Ca, and Sr/Ca maps, which reflect biogenic signals. The U/Ca map clearly illustrates the extent of diagenetic alteration, with the highest concentrations in dentine and at the enamel-dentine junction (EDJ), demonstrating the vulnerability of dental tissues to post-depositional elemental exchange. The Li/Ca map reveals elevated concentrations in both tissues with distinct banding in the enamel. All measurements were obtained using LA-ICP-MS with 40 μm spot size and Ca-normalization to account for matrix effects. b Strontium isotope ratio profiles across H. erectus tooth enamel from Baxian and Naxian caves. LA-MC-ICP-MS 87Sr/86Sr ratio profiles measured along linear transects across tooth enamel from (i) BAX-1 from Baxian Cave, and (ii) NX-A1, (iii) NX-B1, and (iv) NX-B2 from Naxian Cave. The x-axis represents distance in mm along the ablation transect from the cervical region toward the cusp, corresponding to the temporal sequence of enamel formation from early to late childhood. The y-axis shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios, with variation reflecting changes in geological substrate accessed through diet and drinking water during tooth formation. All four individuals exhibit substantial intra-tooth variation in 87Sr/86Sr ratios that exceeds analytical uncertainty, indicating mobility between geologically distinct regions or consumption of resources from multiple locations during childhood. BAX-1 shows 87Sr/86Sr ratios ranging from 0.7110 to 0.7220, while the Naxian specimens display overlapping ranges: NX-A1 (0.7115-0.7165), NX-B1 (0.7095-0.7165), and NX-B2 (0.7100-0.7160). The observed variation patterns provide evidence for landscape mobility of late Middle Pleistocene H. erectus populations in southern China. c Strontium isoscape and geographic assignment probabilities for H. erectus mobility in southern China and northern Southeast Asia. (i) Regional-scale strontium isoscape showing predicted bioavailable 87Sr/86Sr ratios across southern China, northern Vietnam, northern Laos, and adjacent regions. Colours indicate 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.710 (dark blue) to 0.725 (pink), with the Baxian/Naxian cave sites marked by a white dot. Major cities (Hanoi, Lào Cai, Guilin) are shown for geographic reference. (ii) Prediction uncertainty map for the regional isoscape, showing standard error of predicted 87Sr/86Sr values ranging from 0.004 (yellow, low uncertainty) to 0.016 (purple, high uncertainty). (iii) Local-scale isoscape focused on a 400 km × 400 km region centred on the Baxian/Naxian sites, with scale bar representing 50 km. (iv) Prediction uncertainty map for the local isoscape (v-vii) Geographic assignment probability maps for three representative 87Sr/86Sr values observed in H. erectus tooth enamel: (v) Seq1 = 0.714, representing average values for NX-A1 and lower values in NX-B2, showing high assignment probabilities (yellow-green) concentrated within 30-50 km of the cave sites in limestone karst terrain; (vi) Seq2 = 0.719, representing transitional values observed in multiple specimens, showing assignment probabilities extending southward ~150-250 km toward the Red River valley region; (vii) Seq3 = 0.724, representing the most radiogenic values observed (particularly in BAX-1), showing assignment probabilities concentrated in the Red River valley foothills approximately 250 km south of the caves and near Lào Cai to the west, with very low probabilities in the local cave area (dark purple). The progressive southward shift in assignment probabilities from Seq1 to Seq3 indicates long-distance mobility of late H. erectus individuals between the local karst uplands and distant regions up to 250 km away during childhood tooth formation. All isoscapes generated using random forest machine learning based on33 global bioavailable strontium database.

#129462. Raul Jimenez’s late penalty seals share of spoils for Wolves against Blackburn

📅 14 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 27m • 📚 Deep Dive (5426 w)
